title: Georgia’s Government Is Using Civility as an Excuse to Crush Critics
gist: Ani Chkhikvadze reports that Georgia's ruling Georgian Dream party is using February 2026 anti-insult amendments and a new interior-ministry hate-speech unit to fine and jail critics for vulgar online posts, a layer of rapid authoritarian consolidation since the disputed 2024 election. A European Court of Human Rights ruling (Miladze v. Georgia) upholding one such fine has handed the government and other post-Soviet regimes legal cover.

insights.claim: In February 2026 Georgia's parliament amended its Soviet-era Code of Administrative Offenses to punish insults and swearing at officials and public employees, with first offenses fined 1,500-4,000 lari or up to 45 days' detention and repeat offenses up to 6,000 lari or 5-60 days.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Codified speech restrictions deepen Georgia's rule-of-law deterioration and raise governance risk for investors in the country.
insights.locator: His summons is part of a national campaign

insights.claim: Georgia's interior ministry created a 10-person Division for Combating Hate Speech in June that flagged 170 alleged violations and sent 150 cases to court in its first month, yielding 31 fines and two warnings from 33 decisions by July 1.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Proactive state monitoring of social media signals an institutionalized surveillance apparatus rather than episodic repression.

insights.claim: Business owner Zurab Chitaia was fined 3,000 lari (about $1,100) over a Facebook post cursing Georgian Dream, with interior ministry investigators acting without any complaint from an injured party.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Even apolitical business owners face legal exposure for online speech, a chilling factor for Georgia's private sector.
insights.locator: Zurab Chitaia, a Georgian business owner

insights.claim: Prosecuting insults against opposition figures lets Georgian Dream claim even-handed enforcement, but a defense lawyer says government critics receive maximum fines or jail while the other side gets mild penalties.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Selective enforcement dressed as neutrality is a classic hybrid-regime tactic that can blunt Western criticism.

insights.claim: Profane social media criticism has led to jail: activist physician Giorgi Akhobadze was fined 3,000 lari and weeks later sentenced to 25 days of administrative detention.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Escalation from fines to detention marks harsher enforcement.

insights.claim: Crackdowns have sometimes backfired: after blogger Tornike Razmadze was charged for swearing at Kremlin propagandists Margarita Simonyan and Vladimir Solovyov, Georgians flooded social media with insults against Simonyan.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Public defiance suggests the regime's legitimacy remains contested, keeping political instability risk elevated.
insights.locator: The government’s attempts to police online speech

insights.claim: Since the disputed October 2024 election and suspension of EU accession efforts, Georgia has seen mass protests, dozens of prison sentences for protesters, jailed or exiled opposition leaders, and moves by Georgian Dream to ban rival parties.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Georgia's drift from the EU path undermines its appeal as a Western-aligned transit and investment hub in the South Caucasus.

insights.claim: A decade ago Georgia was the democratic leader of the South Caucasus, but it is now moving through the stages of authoritarian consolidation at remarkable speed while trying to keep a democratic facade.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Reassess Georgia country risk; the direction of travel is toward a Russia-leaning hybrid regime.

insights.claim: Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze frames verbal abuse as a weapon of political enemies to destabilize the country and pledges to completely eradicate hate speech.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Security framing of speech suggests further restrictions are likely rather than a rollback.

insights.claim: In May the European Court of Human Rights unanimously ruled in Miladze v. Georgia that a 500-lari fine for a profane TikTok video criticizing Tbilisi's mayor complied with Article 10, distinguishing political criticism from hostile personal denigration.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: The ruling legitimizes Georgia's speech penalties and weakens the European court as a check on the government.
insights.locator: With support from the Georgian Young Lawyers

insights.claim: The Miladze ruling gives other authoritarian governments across the post-Soviet space a Strasbourg precedent to defend penalties for offensive political expression, which would likely fail U.S. First Amendment scrutiny.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Expect the precedent to be cited in speech crackdowns across the region, worsening content-moderation and platform legal risk.
